label: Satellite sensor
short: An instrument passes overhead at night.
known: The VIIRS Day/Night Band records low levels of visible and near-infrared light from orbit, on a regular schedule, at roughly the same local time each night.
assumed: That a pass at around the same hour each night is a fair sample of night-time light in the place.
lost: Anything that happens at other times of night, under cloud, or below the sensor's sensitivity.
whoCanQuestion: Instrument scientists and data providers; anyone who knows when the place is lit and when it is not.

label: Recorded night-time radiance
short: The sensor records how much light reaches it.
known: A radiance value for each observation, in physical units, with flags for cloud, moonlight and other conditions.
assumed: That light reaching the sensor mainly comes from the ground surface below, not from moonlight, aurora, or stray light.
lost: The colour and source of light, which way it points, and whether it is blocked by trees or roofs.
whoCanQuestion: Remote-sensing researchers; lighting engineers; people who know which lights are used here.

label: Processed annual composite / pixel value
short: Many nights become one number per grid cell per year.
known: The provider screens and combines many observations into an annual value for each ~500 m grid cell, following a documented method.
assumed: That the screening removes noise without removing real light, and that methods are comparable across years.
lost: Short events, seasonal patterns, and anything smaller than one grid cell. A year becomes a single average.
whoCanQuestion: Data providers and independent analysts; anyone who can compare the composite with what happened during the year.

label: Observed change over time
short: Comparing years shows the value went up or down.
known: The difference between annual values for the selected area, and which years had limited coverage.
assumed: That the chosen area boundary, start year and end year are meaningful choices — not ones that happen to make a trend look larger or smaller.
lost: Why the change happened. A rise and a dip-and-recovery can produce similar end points.
whoCanQuestion: Anyone reviewing the analysis; people who lived through those years in this place.

label: Possible interpretation
short: Someone proposes what the change might mean.
known: Only that several explanations fit the same signal — see the alternative explanations below.
assumed: That brighter means more activity, more services, or better lives. Research finds night lights relate more closely to electrification and electricity use than to household living standards.
lost: Income, safety, dignity, access to services, local priorities, and whether the people living there would describe this as 'development' at all.
whoCanQuestion: People living in and connected to the place, first. Then researchers, artists, ecologists, and public institutions.

label: Potential action or decision
short: An institution may act on the interpretation.
known: In practice, signals like this are sometimes used to prioritise investment, services, or attention.
assumed: That the interpretation is correct, that the people affected agree, and that the decision-maker has the authority to act.
lost: Consent, local knowledge, and the chance for people affected to say what they actually need.
whoCanQuestion: The people the decision would affect — with access, explanation, and the authority to decide whether and how to respond.
